title: Due Process
hook: Due process is the promise that the state can't take your liberty or property on a whim — it must follow fair, known rules before it acts against you.
key_points: Due process requires the state to follow fair, established procedures before depriving anyone of life, liberty, or property.
Core guarantees: notice of the charge, a fair hearing, and an impartial decision-maker.
It is a practical expression of the rule of law — limits applied to power in individual cases.
It protects everyone, including the unpopular and the guilty, from arbitrary punishment.
content_html: Due process is the principle that the state cannot deprive a person of life, liberty, or property arbitrarily — it must first follow fair, established procedures. It answers a basic worry about power: even a government acting under law could ruin someone simply by skipping the steps, jailing a person with no hearing or seizing property with no chance to respond. Due process closes that gap by insisting that how the state acts against an individual matters as much as what rule it invokes.
extra_html: In practice this means a cluster of procedural guarantees: being told the charge or claim against you (notice), a genuine opportunity to be heard and to contest the evidence (a fair hearing), and a decision made by an impartial authority rather than an interested party. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes the idea traces back centuries to the principle that no one should be punished except "by the law of the land." Due process is, in effect, the rule of law brought down to the level of the individual case — the point where abstract limits on power become concrete protections for a particular person. Crucially, it protects everyone, including the unpopular and even the guilty, because a procedure that can be denied to them can be denied to anyone.

related.title: Civil Liberties Basics
related.hook: The freedoms that protect individuals from overreach by the state — like speech, belief, and a fair trial.

related.title: The Rule of Law
related.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

related.title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
related.hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.

related.title: When DNA Evidence Outlasts the Statute of Limitations
related.hook: A crime can go unprosecuted forever once its statute of limitations runs out — even if DNA later identifies a suspect. Massachusetts is one of the last states moving to close that gap.

flashcards.prompt: What does due process require of the state?
flashcards.back_html: That it follow fair, established procedures — notice, a fair hearing, an impartial decision-maker — before depriving anyone of life, liberty, or property.

flashcards.prompt: Which of these is a core due-process guarantee?

choices.text: Notice of the charge and a fair hearing before an impartial decision-maker
A guarantee that the accused always goes free
The right to choose which laws apply to you

flashcards.explanation_html: Due process is about fair procedure — being told the case against you and getting an impartial hearing — not about guaranteeing any particular outcome.

flashcards.prompt: How does due process relate to the rule of law?

choices.text: It is the rule of law applied to individual cases, limiting arbitrary state action
It replaces the rule of law with official discretion
It applies only to government officials, not ordinary people

flashcards.explanation_html: Due process operationalizes the rule of law case by case, ensuring power is exercised through fair rules rather than arbitrary will.
